sentences.text: This massive animal probably weighed about 5,000 kg, a mass similar to that of a bull African elephant.
Each lower jaw dentary, the main bone of the lower jaw, bears ten teeth.
Where the lower jaws meet at the front, they possess a common chin equaling one-third of the front height.
Researchers concluded the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — was a juvenile because its shoulder girdle bones had not yet fused.
The holotype consists of a partial skeleton including a skull and lower jaws.
The discovery of Mansourasaurus was significant because few Late Cretaceous sauropod remains had been found in Africa.
In 2016, reports indicated that over thirty dinosaur specimens, including titanosaurian sauropods, had been excavated.
The generic name Mansourasaurus refers to Mansoura University.
The specific name shahinae honors Mona Shahin, a founder of the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center.
The existence of Mansourasaurus suggests Africa was less isolated from Eurasian landmasses than previously assumed.
Researchers suggest the ancestors of Mansourasaurus reached Africa from Europe.
The parent group of the genus Mansourasaurus is Diamantinasauria.
Mansourasaurus belongs to the class Saurischia.
Mansourasaurus is classified within Titanosauria as a derived sister species to Lohuecotitan.
Cladistic analysis places Mansourasaurus in a clade with largely Eurasian sauropods including Ampelosaurus, Lirainosaurus, Nemegtosaurus, Opisthocoelicaudia, and Paludititan.
Mansourasaurus is classified as an advanced Titanosauria and is the sister genus to Lohuecotitan.
Mansourasaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, between 83 and 70 million years ago in the Campanian stage, in what is now Africa.
Mansourasaurus is the best-known continental African titanosaur from the Late Cretaceous, specifically the period following the Cenomanian.
Mansourasaurus lived during the Campanian stage, between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
Hypotheses regarding the relationships between Late Cretaceous African and Eurasian sauropods are difficult to test because very few remains have been found in Africa.
